<reason>The debate narrowed to a single decisive question: does abolition reduce Europe's exposure to dubious wealthy migrants, or merely shift them into lighter-screened channels? CON built the stronger path here. Its "other doors" argument (passive-income permits, outright property purchase, company registration) was concrete and PRO's response — a market product vs. discretionary law distinction — was asserted but never defended against CON's rejoinder that those permits carry fixed clocks, immediate Schengen travel, and bank-statement-level vetting. PRO's A2 was a self-inflicted wound: conceding no residency-only failure exists and then arguing that a clean record proves hidden danger gave CON a clean "unfalsifiable standard" hit that it landed twice. PRO's closing attempt to convert "zero marginal exposure" into a confession was cleverly framed but CON correctly showed it points to screening intensity, not to abolition. PRO's best line — the seller-gatekeeper conflict and the fact that every fix needed external EU pressure — was genuinely strong, but CON absorbed it by arguing EU-level oversight is precisely the reform, and that Cyprus's abolition was a proportionate remedy for outright passport sales rather than a template for residency schemes. Both sides had clipped turns (CON twice), which is a real execution cost for CON, but the substantive clash still favored CON's "same people, less scrutiny" frame, which PRO never squarely dismantled.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's B3.1/B4.3 sequence: asking which alternative doors PRO would close, then answering PRO's "discretionary immigration law" distinction by describing passive-income permits as bank-statement tests with fixed naturalization clocks — turning abolition into a reduction in screening rather than a reduction in arrivals. PRO's inability to contest that concretely, combined with the "I can't name one" concession in A4.3, decided the exchange.</best_rebuttal>
